I generally prefer random encounters unless the combat actually takes place on the map like Chrono Trigger.
With on screen encounters i usually end up with the expectation that the dev expects the player to tag every enemy once. Then at that point the encounters start feeling like a chore to me because each troop becomes a part of a check list before moving on to the next map. Not to mention that its not uncommon for them to be placed in 1 tile wide paths and form unavoidable choke points.
I like Etrian Odyssey's approach to it where it uses random encounters primarily, but there are certain enemies on the map with various behaviors that also take a step on the map every turn you take. posts.author: EntangledPear
posts.body:
I prefer random encounters. I might be a weird type of player, though. For me (as a player, and consequently as a developer; I'm lucky I have a partner who deals with that), combat is the least important part of an RPG. So, if there were only on-screen encounters, I'd try to avoid them and then be unprepared for boss battles, which probably wouldn't be avoidable (but, if the game was designed in a way that it was possible to not fight bosses, I'd have no problem having the choice to not fight lesser enemies either). Random encounters force me to gain that EXP and improve those skills, and I'm grateful for that
They may be annoying when I want to explore, but mostly I'm fine with them. I take them as a dev decision and I accept them.

posts.author: Another Fen
posts.body:
Not going to make a definitive statement here.
When it comes to random encounters, there are some things about them that I appreciated in the past.
- The possibility of getting attacked with every step can help making even stepping into a dangerous environment more threatening, even if it is just to grab a chest at the other end of the screen.
- Only getting thrown into combat when I make a move means for me that I don't have to actively press a "pause" button to pause the game if I get distracted for a moment (not that having to pay attention is bad, but it can be nice to have stretches of the game where I don't have to)
- Not showing the details of how I get attacked can mean fewer details that look "off". For example, if visible enemies just run towards your position, a valid strategy could be to run around a wall and watch the enemy get stuck on it, which is fine but can feel a bit ridiculous. Also quite a few games show a remarkable density of large predators roaming their fields just to have enough battle fodder.
But I also feel that you can easily overuse random encounters, especially once the player just starts immediately escaping from all battles if they are not worth fighting. With random encounters I would repeatedly end up in situations where I would watch the battle transition, navigate to the escape option, then run a few more steps into the next battle, all the while listening to the first few seconds of the battle- and field theme on repeat.
Also of course, getting forced into combat and taking damage without any recourse can feel unfair, and I appreciate when the game makes up for it in some way.
You also don't have to stick to either random- or visible encounters I feel. You can still have some random encounters (or "hidden" scripted ones) and have some visible enemies so the areas still look like they are filled with enemies. Visible enemies also offer a lot of possibilities to play around them, like having patrols an observant player can dodge, or an often used "initiative" if you catch an enemy from behind.

As long as the frequency isn't too high; random encounters are my preference.
On screen encounters I feel work best for bosses and such; it makes them more memorable. But having every encounter be on screen always fills me with this odd stress as I now have to weigh if I should try to avoid them or not.
I get why so many people are down on random encounters but as a mechanic it's "fine"; it's not awful and it does its job. posts.author: kirbwarrior
posts.body:
I generally lean random over on screen, but the game itself matters a lot;
Does randomness hamper the experience? On screen. Pokemon is better with on screen encounters because the pokemon are the main point of the series, so being able to
see
them is huge, but also lets you pick them. Dragon Quest (and many,
many
other RPGs) have random drops so being able to choose to fight the enemy with that random drop goes a long way towards sanity.
Is the game built around avoiding encounters? I've seen quite a few rpgs built with the idea that regular encounters are strictly optional. By putting them on screen (and even better, having them not chase you and/or be restricted to 'dangerous' areas like tall grass) helps make that point clear. On the other hand, if the point is to fight a ton of encounters then making them on screen makes it unclear how many you are supposed to fight.
Is there a way to fast travel? One of the main downsides to random (and one some developers put into on screen!) is making it hard to leave a dungeon unfinished because, hey, I was definitely not ready and need to heal. If I can use a skill to get back to town easily, cool. If on screen encounters don't move, it's also easy to get back to town.
Importantly, bad game design can hamper
both
and very easily. RPG MV (and I'm pretty sure a lot of them) uses an absurd (n + n + 1) formula for determining when you'll get into an encounter, where n is a random number between 1 and the encounter step you set. That makes it possible to get into a fight every three steps. I far prefer a setup where the amount of steps is much easier to plan ahead for like with Octopath Traveler (you can count seconds and you'll be off by one at the most). And on screen encounters can be using the regular chase movement built into RPG Maker, which makes it so every enemy chases you down, sometimes at your speed or higher, which can cause the samer issue of battles being back-to-back-to-back-to-back.
What is a "planned" encounter?

posts.author: Maliki79
posts.body:
@kirbwarrior
Planned encounters are encounters that are triggered by events that may or may not be indicated on screen.
So, for example, a planned encounter can be any time a PC moves past say a certain bush on a map.
The event will make a monster jump out of it and attack setting off the encounter.
Chrono Trigger did this a lot.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I prefer random encounters.  For several reasons.
1.  It's no trouble at all to just have an item or tick a box in the options to "lower encounter rate" or "turn encounters off entirely".  Heck, it's what my game does.  The first "Relic" you can get is called "Fear Totem" and if you equip it, encounters are 0.  But, it has the side effect of cutting all your stats in half (so boss fights and unavoidable encounters are harder!).  It's much harder to implement this feature into an on screen format.
2.  The numerous design flaws with on screen encounters brought about by dev laziness.  Too many devs assume "set it and forget it" with this kind of system.  That's wrong.  If you go "on screen encounter" and aren't AT LEAST as good and INNOVATIVE as Earthbound in utility and presentation... don't do it.  You're too lazy to be putting in such a massive system to begin with.
3.  On Screen Encounters have a tendency to make me "fight everything" out of fear I won't be the appropriate level for the bosses.
4.  On Screen Encounters reward you nothing for avoiding them.  In fact, you are often actually hurt more for avoiding them.  Take Pokemon as an example.  There's a Gym in a few of the games where "if you get the right answer" or "if you take the right path", you can avoid trainer fights.  Except, why would you ever WANT to avoid those fights?  You get more XP per Pokemon in a trainer fight than you do with Wild encounters.  You also only get so much money in the game, and it's obtained by defeating trainers.  So, what incentive is there to "get the right answers" and "take the right path"?  There isn't one.  It hurts you if you don't fight these encounters.
---
Breakdown of the design flaws in On Screen Encounters, brought about by laziness.
1.  Presumably these exist to "avoid encounters".  Yet, there are many instances baked into games that use these systems where you can't avoid some combat (narrow hallways, for example).  You also aren't rewarded anything for avoiding the encounters.  So, these systems are actually FORCING THE PLAYER into encounters rather than allowing them TO BE AVOIDED.  It's counter-intuitive... but that's something you expect lazy devs to not notice (they don't do comparisons between the systems, nor do they test play very much to spot the issues in the first place).
2.  On Screen Encounters tend to usually be paired with smaller maps.  Sometimes this is a result of system load.  Sometimes it's a result of devs putting more work into allowing for "escape routes" than "interesting and sprawling" maps.  A hallmark of these games is that usually the maps are pretty small, not much to look at, and those small maps are packed with 3 to 5 encounters.  Compared to the random system where the same small map may be crossed 2 or 3 times without a single encounter, plus has a lot more room to be visually and navigationally more interesting.
3.  Can't usually interact with the sprites on the map.  You can't distract them.  They don't run away if you're too powerful.  You can't force specific encounters with them.  Can't weaken them before a fight.  You need to at least do as much with them as Earthbound does.  Almost no dev ever does anything except "set it and forget it".
4.  Rarely ever AI attached to enemies except "here's its movement pattern" or "it always moves toward you".  This takes a lot of work and will undoubtably make the feature more interesting and make the act of engaging or avoiding the enemies more engaging.  But... again... lots of work.  Most devs aren't willing to put forth the work to do this.
5.  Troop composition tends to be less interesting, when it's almost always "static".  This encounter is always this troop composition.  Etcetera.  So, troop compositions tend to be on the sparse side with combat itself tending to suffer from mechanical stagnancy.  In a On Screen encounter system, you tend to find about 5-6 troop compositions per encounter.  This means, at most you can expect to encounter 2 mechanics per dungeon.  With no iteration on those mechanics.
---
Anyway, that's what I got.
I tend to prefer random encounters because they tend to have one problem (encounter rate too high), compared to on screen, which typically has many instances of "this is not even half baked".
The shorthand is this:
Do you want fast food that is always of the same tasty quality, though not very good for you... Or do you want an elaborate 3 course meal that takes 12 hours to make... ultimately prepared by the same fast food worker with no cooking experience beyond dropping fries into the oil?
I await the day someone actually makes an amazing On Screen encounter system.  Because, the person who pulls that off will be a legend and the new standard for those, which will dethrone Earthbound.  They will possibly have the greatest RPG of all time because they were willing to put in the time and effort to make their game be that way.
Until then, I'm just not a fan of having to engage with On Screen encounter games.  I usually count such systems as a point against the games since they have a tendency to be a good indicator of "slop" these days.  Just like, "amazing graphics!".

Interesting perspective.  Here is a system that would incorporate some of what everyone is saying:
Random Encounters
- (medium rewards) diminishing chance of appearance over time as regional victory and quest count increases.  Enemies have a starting level and may scale upward slightly as character level increases or as region victory count increases.
On-Screen Encounters
- (low rewards) these propagate from spawning sources.  As such, they repeat spawn over time.  Players will usually prefer to avoid them.  Dungeons, mini dungeons, quests, places, or characters/monsters can serve as spawners.  Clearing a spawning source removes the on-screen obstacle encounters they generate.
On-Screen Hunts/Mini-Bosses
-  (high rewards) one-time enemies that appear automatically or conditionally.  There are not too many... and they can be hard to find.  Players will want to defeat them all but don't need to.
Fixed Encounters
- (variable rewards) This includes game bosses and  invisible 'forced' encounters.  They are generally unavoidable using map movement techniques and are built in to the storyline.

You might want to define what those rewards are and how they fit together.  What I might define as a "low reward", you might define as "medium reward".  For me, a great many rewards in a great many games count as "low rewards".  For example, if it just drops like 5% more XP than everything else here... that's what I'd consider an outlier, rather than a whole tier up in terms of rewards.  A jump of 200% currency might also be considered "a low reward" to me, if money in your game is... useless and I'm already carrying like 500,000 of the stuff with nothing to spend it on.
I'll see if I can point out the flaws of each of these proposals (stuff you'll have to keep in mind if you plan to implement these)
Random Encounters
Removal of grinding for XP/Currency rarely ever goes well.  Just based on what you've put in here...  Basically the winning move is "only fight enough to get the best equipment, then avoid as much combat as possible".  It's my usual Go-To move for these types of systems.  Break the game by refusing to play by its rules.  You primarily get most of your stats from equipment in an RPG anyway, rather than levels, so it's more useful to bypass any system that would inevitably punish me for grinding levels and getting a few extra points into my critical stats (on average, in most RPG's, you need 3 levels to equal one Tier of equipment up from where you are).  A lot of devs don't really realize how much power they're granting by level versus equipment (nor do they do a lot of side by side comparisons of it), so they erroneously believe that "limiting level grinding" is how you fix difficulty in their games.
The truth of that is:  If having bigger stats on my characters trivializes your combat... it was never "that good" to begin with, nor "that hard".
On-Screen Encounters
This is... a double-edged sword.  On the one hand, to get rid of an annoyance, a player would wipe it out first.  On the other hand, once it's gone, you can't grind levels here anymore if you want to.  Or get currency.  Or item drops.  You're offering a permanent solution to a temporary problem.  One that probably isn't going to feel very "fun" to a player.
On-Screen Hunts/Mini-Bosses
This could work, but you have to be careful.  These usually turn into Guide-Dang-It affairs.  Especially for completionists.  But, these can also affect players who are in it "for the skill".  Something a dev feels is optional has to be designed VERY CAREFULLY so that it FEELS OPTIONAL to a player.
Let me tell you, as a completionist, anything that resembles a "checklist" item, forces me to go out of my way to do it.  I only get around this with Achievements in games by never looking at the achievement list.  But, the moment I know there's a list of some kind... guess how my gameplay changes and how my enjoyment changes alongside it?
Optional content isn't usually that "optional" for some players.
"you don't have to do it" from a dev often turns into me saying "well, you didn't have to add it in, either, then did you?"  Truly optional content can be removed and not impact the fun of anyone playing the game.  But, the truth is, it often does.  One way or another.
Fixed Encounters
Yeah, this is just the standard for most games.  Even non-RPG ones.

posts.author: EsoStrix
posts.body:
At the moment random encounters are a staple to my game, but as I've experimented more and more with eventing I've definitely tried mixing it up a bit with different areas.
For example in one area of my game the enemies are more 'passive' (for story reasons), so instead of battles happening at random in that area, I made roaming enemies that you can avoid by waiting for them to pass, but any contact with them will initiate a battle.
I've also used the bubbling graphics in water and lava levels to indicate potential threats, so going near a bubble will make an enemy jump out and attack you for example.

2.  On Screen Encounters tend to usually be paired with smaller maps.  Sometimes this is a result of system load.  Sometimes it's a result of devs putting more work into allowing for "escape routes" than "interesting and sprawling" maps.  A hallmark of these games is that usually the maps are pretty small, not much to look at, and those small maps are packed with 3 to 5 encounters.  Compared to the random system where the same small map may be crossed 2 or 3 times without a single encounter, plus has a lot more room to be visually and navigationally more interesting.
3.  Can't usually interact with the sprites on the map.  You can't distract them.  They don't run away if you're too powerful.  You can't force specific encounters with them.  Can't weaken them before a fight.  You need to at least do as much with them as Earthbound does.  Almost no dev ever does anything except "set it and forget it".
4.  Rarely ever AI attached to enemies except "here's its movement pattern" or "it always moves toward you".  This takes a lot of work and will undoubtably make the feature more interesting and make the act of engaging or avoiding the enemies more engaging.  But... again... lots of work.  Most devs aren't willing to put forth the work to do this.
5.  Troop composition tends to be less interesting, when it's almost always "static".  This encounter is always this troop composition.  Etcetera.  So, troop compositions tend to be on the sparse side with combat itself tending to suffer from mechanical stagnancy.  In a On Screen encounter system, you tend to find about 5-6 troop compositions per encounter.  This means, at most you can expect to encounter 2 mechanics per dungeon.  With no iteration on those mechanics.
---
Anyway, that's what I got.
I tend to prefer random encounters because they tend to have one problem (encounter rate too high), compared to on screen, which typically has many instances of "this is not even half baked".
The shorthand is this:
Do you want fast food that is always of the same tasty quality, though not very good for you... Or do you want an elaborate 3 course meal that takes 12 hours to make... ultimately prepared by the same fast food worker with no cooking experience beyond dropping fries into the oil?
I await the day someone actually makes an amazing On Screen encounter system.  Because, the person who pulls that off will be a legend and the new standard for those, which will dethrone Earthbound.  They will possibly have the greatest RPG of all time because they were willing to put in the time and effort to make their game be that way.
Until then, I'm just not a fan of having to engage with On Screen encounter games.  I usually count such systems as a point against the games since they have a tendency to be a good indicator of "slop" these days.  Just like, "amazing graphics!".

I know most RPG's have it be common that you walk up and talk to the boss in the last room, but I don't always do that.  Sometimes, it's just surprise boss time! The halved stats for quests and dialogue choices was just a "happy accident".  But, I figured players would unequip the totem in towns anyway, so not too huge of an issue.

I just didn't think it was worth it to try to 3000% police usage of an item like the Fear Totem.  Or, agonize over how to design it better.  Instead, I mostly just embraced allowing the player to "exploit" the game, sometimes.  And, other times, the game would exploit them for using it.
But, that's sort of the understanding I want the player to come away with in terms of mechanics in my game.  I want the player to know that they are ALLOWED to get away with stuff. It's part of a series of items called "Relics".  They work like "Traits" in Fallout New Vegas, or earlier Fallout games.  Get a positive and a negative that alters your playstyle.
These are given out through trading "Diamonds" to an NPC.  The first one is part of a choice.  You can choose the Fear Totem.  Or, you can choose the "Blemished Coin".  The coin doubles Gold gain from combat, but halves your encounter rate.
So, it's entirely possible that a player wouldn't even pick the Fear Totem on a run of the game.  And yes, players can exploit the coin by only equipping it for boss fights or other static encounters.
I just didn't think the possible exploit was really something that needed to be prevented, much as I might want to guarantee "consequences" for using it.
Especially since there are things locked behind gaining levels.  If you skip too much combat, you do miss lessons that bosses will test you on (each enemy formation is designed to teach you a trick, or an overpowered way to win, or even how your old strategies will no longer work).
I just didn't think the effort to punish players for overuse would be worth what I wanted them to learn (namely to unequip it when they didn't need it).
Plus, the game is very "resource management" heavy in its execution.  No Dedicated Healers, so you have to buy items to heal (or visit an Inn).  One of the earliest things I teach is "if you are out of half your resources and you aren't at the boss room yet, you need to head back out of the dungeon and buy some more".
You can, theoretically, skip every enemy in the Poison Dungeon.  But, if you don't accumulate enough money to buy Antidotes, you will be merc'd by the Boss of the dungeon.  A boss which basically poisons you with every attack.  Poison at that stage in the game, also dealing as much damage as being hit with a regular attack.
A lot of the game is sort of built this way.  Very few things have "direct and immediate punishments".  Planning and Prep are the name of the game.  Failure to do these things, usually results in a game over.

I suppose if you want to denegrate game design, calling it "coddling" is an option. It's sort of missing the forest for the trees.
This decision was made because at the core of my game is:
A low stress game.
A game the emphasizes player approach.
A sense of "slice-of-life" with cozy-but-not-empty game design decisions.
At the core of the game's design, these philosophies are followed every step of the way.
So visible enemy troops fits into this design philosophy.
Were I designing Dark Souls with practically opposite design philosophy, I would likely consider how troops are handled entirely differently.
The fact of the matter is that a good game developer is considering what their game is trying to achieve through it's design philosophy and will make decisions based around that. It's actually a very important part because it helps you narrow down who your target audience is, and if you want a successful game, you're gonna need to know who your player should be. Joe-blow who wants old skool DQ and FF is not my target audience, and so in all likelihood, will not like my design decisions. However, Susan-sue who likes Atelier games or Stardew Valley, will really enjoy the decisions I've made for my game's design.
We often say "it depends" when it comes to game design questions because this is exactly why. It just depends on the type of game you are making, the philosophies you have in mind for it's design, and who your target audience is. It makes seemingly simple decisions like "random encounter? on map encounters?" a difficult question that you really should be deeply considering.

(RND) - One of each local. Limit of first one per type.  2x EXP, victory: decrease region penalty by 2%, decrease region encounter rate by 5 steps.  Initial encounter rate = 5 steps. [No Escape.  Can avoid with creep speed.]
LOCAL
(RND) - Repeats (not shock)  1/2 EXP.  [can escape. Penalty when party is running]
WORLD
(RND) - One of each global from matching type (land, sea, space, alien, dungeon) Chance of WORLD encounter is 1% override on random encounter.  Goes up .25% per world victory and per level.
Adds escalating flat EXP bonus.  Permanantly increases EXP bonus by 1%.  [Escape is allowed.]
PATROL
(on map) - up to 3 of these guard each Dungeon entrance area.  Routes and behaviors vary.  Most are respawning until dungeon has been cleared. [No Ecape]
BOUNTY
(on map) - one per region.  Respawn as Next Higher Level after a period of time, or conditionally. (approximately 4 tiers per region).  High EXP. awards 2% to 5% EXP boost) [can Escape]
BOSS
(fixed) -  One time. similar to bounty, except needed for progression or Dungeon clear. [no escape]  High EXP.  Awards vary.  Victory typically defines dungeon a quell, and removes patrols.

posts.body:
Canned_Dinosaur said:
May I kindly suggest you give it a rest? This sort of verbal defecating on a certain mechanic is guaranteed to incite negative responses. The hardest games I've played so happened to feature on-map encounters. So aside from not agreeing to your choice of words, I also disagree with your statement that on-map encounters make a play through easier.
Click to expand...
I'm... not sure what the argument is even about at this point.  Everyone is just talking passed each other and nobody is really making any valid points on their points of view (though they do appear to be trying really, really hard to be!).
There is always the choice, every person has, to not make a negative reply to something someone says.
Though, the way I define "negative replies" and the way others do might differ (a negative reply is when someone gets upsetti spaghetti, throws logic and reason out the window, and then proceeds to attack the person, rather than the ideas, to my definition.  I do notice others define it as "you disagree with me, stop being negative!", however).
For your reply here, I could argue that the on-map encounters do make playthroughs easier.  For a variety of reasons.  But, those reasons would only be compared to the random encounters.  And, those reasons would ignore that almost all RPG combat is basically easy mode anyway.  With very few and very rare exceptions.  Most often because devs are too lazy or inept to properly balance their games, or even design combat very well (stat stick central!).
But, "easy" and "difficult" are also self-defined.  What you find difficult, I might find easy.  And, the reverse applies.
Once I got into the FromSoft games (or Dark Souls-like), I discovered that... these are some of the easiest games I've ever played.  But, I seem to play them differently than everyone else.  I play in the way of "you do anything you can to win".  If you don't stick to strict build mandates, you will rofl-stomp almost every encounter.  If you read item descriptions, experiment, and change up tactics frequently when you die, you will have no difficulty in these games.
But, then you get players who are like, "I must parry everything!" and "I must block everything!" and "I need to learn the boss mechanics!".  For those players, sure these games are hard.  For players unwilling to inflict status effects on bosses (or enemies), unwilling to use magic, or unwilling to use ranged attacks...  These games are difficult.  For players who refuse to use melee combat and only use magic or ranged attacks... these games are difficult.  Players who refuse to adapt or change their play style have a rough time in these games.
A player like me, however, takes the storylines of these games to heart.  You do anything you can to win.  Because that's what everyone else in these games' lore is doing.
The difference in these players might also mean they have fun in different ways.  The parry and block crowd might really love learning patterns and "playing perfectly" to that extent.  That's what they're into.  Nothing wrong with that.  Personal preference in how you decide you're going to play is not "overall reflection of difficulty" in the slightest.  Just because a player prefers to play suboptimally, doesn't mean a game is difficult.  It just means playing their specific way, is difficult.
As a dev, this is important information to know.  Is the game difficult because you only plan for players to play your game in one very specific way?  Or, is it difficult, because there is no other way for the players to play your game?
"Combat in FF13 is difficult", I once had the pleasure of debating.  I countered by saying, "No, it's easy.  I basically bypassed the stagger meter every opportunity I could, and overleveled at every moment the game would let me.  Then, I got access to summons, and a means to use them in basically every single battle... and the stagger meter became pointless.".  I played the game in a way nobody else was doing, apparently.
Lies of P.  "Difficult Souls-like".  Oh, is it?  Rather than engage with all the parry and other mechanics I hated, I just defeated every single boss with throwables.  With the exception of the first boss, which I ended up just cheesing its AI to give me openings.  I never learned how to perfect block or parry.  I barely ever even used "block" in the game, except against standard mooks.
"Difficulty" is subjective personal opinion most of the time.  You might think you're designing a difficult game.  But, then someone like me comes along and just bypasses all the nonsense you think would make it difficult, and you make it SO EASY TO BYPASS, that I would label your game "easy" and that you might "coddle the player too much".
Though, that's a decently incendiary thing to say.  You might not have intended to coddle the player.  Or make it so easy.  You might have intended the game to be played contrary to how I play it, and expected all the players to read the script you provided, and play their part.  Which, is valid.  But, you need to understand how players can break your systems and how easy that often is to do.  How easy is it for me to go off script, never learn your lessons you're trying to teach me, and I can still win?
That's how you determine "true difficulty".  The ease with which the players can win the game without learning all the lessons you are trying to teach them (or any of the lessons).
Give you a few hints:
1.  Most devs forget that they're giving their players a constant influx of money and items.  Money which can be used to buy items.  Items which turn out to be "effective HP".  As in, if you have 100 HP, and 5 potions of "heals 50 HP", your player now has 350 HP instead.  If you have items that double attack power for 3 turns, your players don't have 180 attack... they have 360 attack.  Especially if they can buy those items.  Or farm them.  The item ecnomy is something you ALWAYS have to consider.  Most players are too dim (or stubborn) to utilize items in this way.  But, you need to account for it!  For the players who aren't!
2.  Synergy between skills/items matters!  Final Fantasy X had some fun exploits I used.  One of which was the "mix" command, where you could get very common items that basically mixed into "bad breath" skills thrown at enemies/bosses.  Very quick way to take down most enemies.  Especially if you changed the way the meter filled to "each attack" and then just jacked up Rikku's speed stat with things like Haste so she was getting 8-12 attacks before an enemy gets 1.  You could also save the "mix" command for usage against bosses on the first turn.  The other exploit I paired with it was throwing Auron into Rikku's path so that even though he was "a heavy", he became a lightning bruiser which broke most of the game (he initially has the highest amount of attack/strength orbs in the game on his path, but he's so slow that he often acts once per every other characters twice...  But, he also has "piercing" as his skill... so he can effectively maul every enemy in the game with high enough speed and attack, and if he's getting 4 or 5 attacks to every 1 the enemy gets... super broken!  A lot of devs don't account for stuff like this.  They don't account for players getting things early.  Or using things in "unconventional" ways.
3.  Limiting what the player can do may lead to them min/maxing, and making the game easier.  Fallout New Vegas.  Hardcore mode.  Made me prioritize carry weight, and so any perk related to that.  Also made me prioritize any perk that made my pistol and shotgun more broken.  Forced me to not carry around half a dozen guns either, and learn how to play Caravan.  Caravan was more lucrative than the casinos and required no luck, and barely any skill to win.  With a weight limit that penalized me so hard, I carried two pistols and 1 shotgun.  I sold all ammo for everything else, and all guns.  I could literally buy my way to the end of the game.  And one-shot even cazadores by the end.  The previous run was actually harder as I hadn't focused my build or gameplay so much.  But, with all the restrictions imposed on me by "Hardcore", I min/maxed into being stupidly broken.  Pokemon nuzlocke challenges have a similar issue.  "It's a hard challenge!".  Not really.  Infinite heals at a Pokemon center anytime you need them, and then you just severe over level... easiest challenge ever as you'll win most fights with a 10+ level advantage and never really be in danger of losing any mons except to random luck.
4.  Minimum viable level and maximum attainable level are things you need to consider.  If I don't need to fight every encounter in your game to win, because I've got awesome equipment or a lot of items...  Then I can skip most of your encounters.  There's a reason a lot of shooters make it "difficult" to bypass fights.  If a player can bypass fights in an RPG... there might be similar issues going on.  If a player can't bypass a fight, then you need to consider the maximum attainable power the player can achieve at that point in the game (I usually account for 3-5 hours of a player grinding on top of everything they have access to at the moment), because that's what players are going to be doing if they have any difficulty at all, or if they're farming for a drop or something.
---
Difficulty is subjective.
If a user is telling you, "designing a game this way makes it easier for me to beat your game and bypass all challenge", it's something you should consider in your design.
Likewise, if a user is saying, "I find games that have this to be usually more difficult", then that's also something to consider in the design of the game, too.
As for me?
I don't understand the argument of difficulty.  Everyone talks about how difficult a game is or is meant to be.  Nobody talks about HOW MUCH FUN the game is.
Some games, that are super easy, are a ton of fun.  Some games, that are very difficult, are a ton of fun.
Difficulty doesn't matter if your game isn't fun to begin with.
Largely, I find on-map encounters to be "anti-fun" due to poor dev design and planing.  I find them to be more tedious than random encounters.

To be fair, you have this same issue with on-screen encounters.  Without a method to "turn off encounters", this ends up just being a failure for both systems.  Backtracking, in general, should be made decently interesting to the player, if you're making the player do it at all (I prefer how Metroidvanias do it, where you now can unlock new paths, or approach old areas in new ways where you can blaze through them so much faster. I can only partially agree with what you're saying.  Mostly because I think the topic is more nuanced than you feel it is.  It's why I made the argument about "difficulty" and it "being subjective".
I'll address the points you quoted from yourself.  Hopefully that might make things a little more clear.
deus69xxx said:
i stand by coddling, the game is easy mode when it's 'on map' encounters. you pick and choose what and when, have every opportunity to plan with precisely how many, without the pure chaos of accidental ambushes, nothing becomes risky. you can go through most of chrono trigger without any attacks (which is a bad idea before new game +), mystic quest allowed you to restart fights until you win (if possible at your level), etcetera. it got even worse when save anywhere came out in some of them, though i agree with that for mobile.
Click to expand...
I honestly want an explanation of why you think this is "coddling".  Now, I can guess why you think it is so.  I did so the first time.  My assumption was that "you can avoid any encounters you don't want to engage in, and save your resources".  But, this is really only a "partial answer".
Why is that a bad thing?
You state later that "resource management" type gameplay is "part of the challenge".  Isn't evading enemies part of that resource management?  Isn't that smart and skilled play?  To preserve resources you don't need to spend, to beat the boss?
If you don't feel it is, why not?
Likewise, why is "restarting the fight" if you lose a bad thing?  This is something built into every RPG, ever.  You lose the fight, game over, restart from save point, have to do the fight again anyway.  I feel that allowing you to "restart the fight" at the point of loss is a nice feature to have to avoid backtracking and "get right back into the action, knowing what you did wrong last time".
I'm also unclear why you dislike "save anywhere".  At worst, it's used to "savescum".  But, that's an easy workaround (I have two in my own game for skill checks, but allow players to save scum their dialogue choices, since the point isn't that the player makes "good" choices, but instead "choices they can live with".  Many of my "moral high ground" choices have unintended consequences that a player may not enjoy.  It ain't easy to be a "goody two shoes" in my game.).  I much prefer "save anywhere", since as an adult, I often have to quit a game "partway through gameplay".  Saving anywhere allows me to put down the game at any time and come back to it later when I can.  I think the benefits far outweigh any detriments, and you can always quickly and easily program ways around "savescumming" if you care enough.
deus69xxx said:
the only real excitement in those games is the story. the difficulty, the... terror of all your progress being undone by some over eager group of monsters killing your party in the bowels of werdna's dungeon... that's all undone, because you have a 100 percent chance to just 'nope' out of it before it ever happens.
Click to expand...
Eh... to my opinion, the only reason you play an RPG is for the story.  Anything else is "tertiary" to keep you invested in the story, and give you a sense of progression through the world (and as enough of a skilled warrior to beat the final boss, so that it's believable).
But, this opinion is heavily steeped in "most combat in RPG's just simply isn't fun in the slightest, anyway.  It's either basic or pointlessly overcomplicated.  It rarely rewards clever players, as you don't need to be clever in most games to win, and its way of calling you 'clever' is just using Water on the Fire Monster.".
In my 30+ years of gaming and playing RPG's, I've yet to find one that "makes me feel skilled" or "clever" or "accomplished" in combat.  It's all either "unreasonable struggles that take too long" or "watch Netflix while I play".  Engagement in combat for me is basically non-existent most of the time.  Probably because devs who design RPG's don't take pages out of other game genres for "making the gameplay interesting".  Like, why is it fun to solve puzzles with Portals, but not really to push rocks around and onto switches?  Why is it awesome to engage in combat in F.E.A.R. or Halo, and make you want to do it all the time... but in an RPG, it's boring?
My theory is there's just "not enough choice and interactivity" in RPG combat to make it as interesting or engaging.  The AI in F.E.A.R. is actually really super basic and easy to manipulate, but it doesn't feel that way.  Why?  Callouts.  The enemy makes a lot of callouts that make it FEEL LIKE they're really smart.  Likewise, they're also very specifically designed to use the portions of the level they fill, in specific ways (like, literally scripted to flank and such, or throw a grenade at you when you're behind a specific piece of cover, or whatever).  Halo has something similar with its callouts.  You can tell when enemies get angry.  They callout to each other.  They freak out.  Their behaviors change sometimes (an angry elite will charge you with no regard for its own safety.  A pack of grunts that loses its leader attempts to flee or hide.  Etcetera.).
That theory has lead me to design my enemies with "gimmicks" instead of "stats".  Because I remember things like, "Thunder stun all dinosaur, you know?" and how that changed up gameplay for me, and how it became memorable.  Well, you know what?  "All wolves run from fire.  Try burning them!" and "Strong monsters or Leaders often get angry when you exploit their weaknesses.  Be careful for retaliation!".  Among a ton of other things.  On top of which, my players are just handled a "toolbox" and they get to choose how and where and when they use what's in it.  Which allows them some easy victories sometimes.  Or, anytime they can figure out how to get an easy victory out of that box.
I think "solve the puzzle" combat in an RPG is infinitely more interesting when you can provide answers that are "hit it with a sledgehammer really hard" as well as "learn the attack pattern and avoid all damage".
Or, at least... this type of combat is my answer to "RPG combat has never been interesting or engaging to me in more than 30 years of gaming".  At least it's something different, to my opinion.
deus69xxx said:
there's a distinction to be made between game design approaches. you don't want the difficulty to be at a certain average level that requires investment in your game akin to the origins of the genre, fine, i won't argue it, but it's still essentially giving your players (in a way) a free ride. yes, the story may be awesome, which is certainly part of it, but at that point, you could just write a book. the fight for that next part of the story is the key, my friends... that's 30% of the reason to play.
Click to expand...
I'm afraid this is mostly just arguing for your own preferences in game design.  Which, on its own, is fine.
The problem is likely the "blanket statement" of "giving your players a free ride".  This goes back to my post on "difficulty is subjective personal opinion".  I think all of Elden Ring and Dark Souls is "a free ride" just due to the sheer number of resources available and combat options to clear any boss or challenge with ease (I die more to falling off of things than any boss in any of these games, due to my nature of using everything, and not over-specializing as a player).  But, that's because I play in my own specific way, which makes the game easy for me.  And, gosh darn it, if everyone WOULD JUST PLAY EXACTLY LIKE ME, they'd see the game is easy, too!
They really would.
But, playing the way I do might not be fun for a lot of those players.  After all, a good chunk of that playerbase routinely spouts that they "play it because it's hard".  "Git Gud" and all that.  "It's tough, but fair".  On and on.  They also call me a "coward" in terms of how I play, or "unskilled", or whatever else.  "You didn't struggle, therefore your win isn't valid".  Or whatever.
That's just the nature of games.
I think playing Smash Bros on the flattest most generic, boring, no level hazard maps with all items off is "not competitive play" and "is not very skilled at all, as it doesn't test adaptability, situational awareness, or even clever item usage", but do you think many who play that genre in tournaments would agree with me?  Probably not.  In this instance, I might be "right", but at the same time, the way I want them to play would "ruin the fun" for them, correct?
What I find difficult and fun is subjective personal opinion.  Same for other players of the same games.
But, that's why we gamedev.  So we can design the games we want to play.  With the underlying philosophies we believe in.  And, hopefully, find an audience for our own weird preferences and idiosyncracies.
---
As an aside, creating a story for a game is not the same as writing a book.  It realy isn't.  The closest it comes to anything writing related is "writing a stage play".
I would know, I do a lot of writing.  One of the reasons I got interested in making games was because telling a story through them was unlike anything I'd ever written or read before, and seemed a unique challenge.  Especially when the players can "contribute" to that story as well, rather than just experience it.
It's also not really "the fight for the next part of the story".  It's usually the part of the story that is "show, don't tell" that keeps the player there.  The combat is part of that story, if it's done well.  You can claim a location is dangerous all you want. Let's put that in perspective for you.
The average amount of "encounters" per dungeon across all RPG's is around 25-35 (depending on dungeon length and backtracking required).  On average, each encounter will usually furnish the player with enough currency to afford 4-10 consumables (of relevant tier to HP/MP usage).  On average, most players will expend 2-3 consumables every 2-3 encounters.
So, at the worst rates, you'll get enough currency to pay for 100 consumables, and expend 36 total consumables (4 consumables for 25 encounters.  100 total consumables.  Spend 3 consumables every 2 encounters, so 25/2=12.  Multiply by 3.  36 total consumables used).
How are we "losing resources" exactly?  This is just "effective HP" and "effective MP".
It gets even funnier when you consider that MP used per point of health healed is usually a 1 to 10 ratio in RPG's... and that even at a double price for an MP potion versus an HP potion, you are paying far less for HP heals via MP than you would get via an HP potion.
You don't even usually need to expend a combat action to heal either (since enemies deal so little damage in combat)!  So, it's all just "effective HP" and "no losses".
You have to use an unreasonable amount of your consumables every fight, in almost every RPG, to actually "lose" anything.
It's rare you'll ever use all 99 Potions and 99 MP Potions every dungeon, or even between dungeons.  You'll use maybe 30, hit up town, restock, and then back to the next fight, not really down anything.  You could tackle like 3 dungeons on a stock of 99, and then afford like 40 Inn stays AND a full refill of both HP and MP potions by the time they ran out!
This is why I say you have to treat your consumables as "effective HP/MP".  Because, they are.  If your player is walking into each dungeon with an extra 4950 HP and MP in their back pocket... you have to do a lot of damage to them to whittle that down to make the dungeon "dangerous" in the slightest.  Or, if it's late game, the player might be walking into the dungeon with 29700 extra HP/MP in their back pockets!
Encounters aren't about "resource management" unless the player actually loses resources for poor play.  And no, I don't mean "they use a Potion".  I mean, "they use a Potion and don't make enough money back from winning the fight to buy another one".
By the by
that's how my game works
Players attain mastery in combat so they stop expending resources and can start stockpiling them.  It is very possible to "soft lock" yourself in my game by playing very poorly and mismanaging your cash.  Especially since most equipment is attained from shops.  And it costs significantly more than healing items.
For perspective:
Healing Powder:  Heals 30 HP.  Costs 20 Currency.
First Sword Upgrade:  +3 Damage.  Costs 65 Currency.
Basic Slime Enemies:  Drop 1 XP and 1 Currency.  Deals 1 or 2 damage to you on hit (with basic armor).
First Dungeon Enemies Average:  4 XP and 3 Currency.  Deals 3-5 damage to you on hit (with basic armor).
You start with only 20 HP.  Leveling up does not give you more HP.  You need to complete a quest that awards HP, to get more HP.
You need to defeat 20 slimes for 1 Healing Powder... or 7 enemies in the first dungeon to afford 1 Healing Powder.  Do the math.
Makes it sound like my game has enemies that are "there to drain your resources", right?  Except, no.  Their purpose is to train you how to fight the boss.  To teach you how to take no damage.  Or minimal damage.  Because, I harshly punish ANY mistake the player makes.
Loss of resources is my way of telling the player, "you F'd up, bad.".  Stockpiling your resources is my way of saying, "doing a great job, keep it up!".
So, yes, allowing my players to "bypass the enemy fights there is nothing left to learn from" is something I don't mind them doing.  Player Characters are wiped in 5 hits anyway.  You get 5 mistakes.  That's it.
The lesson to the player is "if you want the ability to mitigate more mistakes, you need to make almost no mistakes".
Oh, and no, I rarely ever have currency in random chests.
And would you believe that the combat isn't even really the point of my game, either?  It's Narrative Driven/Focused.
I had to take into account a LOT of systems, how they work, and how players interact with them.  Especially with Dedicated Healers removed, levels no longer granting direct power (but indirect power), resources being scarce, heavy focus on changing equipment and making player choices, heavy focus on storyline and character interactions with each other, and an idea to make "almost any encounter winnable with nearly any stats, as long as you play well".
The combat has been the hardest part to balance and ensure my design philosophy stays in.
The "players can turn off encounters" is the LEAST of my worries.  It is, by far, the most miniscule thing I'll ever have to worry about, because it matters so little to the overall gameplay loop and expectations I have placed upon my players.
Possible exploitation and "making the game easier" by turning off encounters in my game isn't really much of a problem or concern.  Not when the bosses wipe you in 5 hits, because you learned nothing.
Anyway, tangent over.  If you aren't accounting loss of consumables against currency gained, and accounting those excess consumables as "extra HP/MP", then your game is likely going to be super easy.
Especially for players like me.
I certainly have never minded every RPG since the NES days giving me 27,000 health once I reach level 10, in which to beat every single dungeon.

One system I thought was really cool was 'limited' random encounters where each map had a certain number of fights you'd get into total before they stopped forcing you into battle (say, 20 on this map, 14 on that map, the number never resets on a given map). In addition, you can press a button on the controller to force a random encounter to let the player grind and to fight after that number ran out.
